newsitem.title: JAPAN: Future optimistic for Japan stocks - Morgan Stanley.
newsitem.headline: Future optimistic for Japan stocks - Morgan Stanley.

text.p: The future for Japan's stock market is optimistic but recent declines in prices have created a serious situation, Morgan Stanley's chief global strategist Barton Biggs said in a lecture on Tuesday.

Biggs told journalists and officials from financial firms that Morgan Stanley was one of few institutions in the world with assets that are slightly overweight in Japan and much more overweight in the rest of Asia.
Asked how he viewed the recent moves in the Japanese stock market, he said: "The situation is serious."
"We are quite pessimistic about U.S. in the next 12 months," he added.

"Stock and bond markets are trying to tell politicians and the Ministry of Finance that two percent is too much," Biggs said of the scheduled two-percentage point rise in Japan's consumption tax from the current three percent on April 1.
He also said the markets are rightfully worried about the government's fiscal programme.
Biggs said the profitability of Japanese firms at present was not good, but added that their stock prices were "reasonable" when compared with the yield of government bonds.

With the Price Book-Value Ratio (PBR) of Japanese stocks having fallen to just below two times, the stocks cannot be called undervalued by international standards, but are reasonably priced given their historical performance in Japan, he said.
He said it would not be surprising if it took 15 years for the Nikkei average to surpass its historical high of about 39,000.
But Biggs added: "Morgan Stanley is very optimistic about Japan and the growth of Japan and about the Japanese stock market."
Concerning U.S. stocks, he said the bull market would continue for a little while longer but added that the U.S. stock market's bull run was in its "seventh or eighth inning".
He said the U.S. stock market was currently in a "bubble" stage and expressed concern that the possible bursting of the bubble in the future could have an impact on the economy.
The U.S. public is much more involved in the stock market now than the Japanese public was during Japan's late-1980s bubble era.
Regarding the yen, Biggs said it could weaken further to 125 to 130 against the dollar.
"The depreciation of the yen is not over with," he said.
He said the current situation was that the yen was weak and not that the dollar was strong. This was because of the current Japanese economic situation, he said.
